Vaka Dālbhya (‘descendant of Dalbha’) is the name of a teacher in the Chāndogya upaniṣad. According to the kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, he was engaged in a ritual dispute with dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Foot notes i. 2, 13; 12, 1.
xxx. 2 (Indische Studien, 3, 471).

Vakala denotes in the Brāhmaṇas the ‘inner bark’ of a tree, ‘bast.’
Foot notes taittirīya brāhmaṇa, iii. 7, 4, 2; kauṣītaki brāhmaṇa, x. 2.

Vakṣaṇā, fem. plur. denotes in one passage of the Rigveda the bed of a stream.
Foot notes iii. 33, 12. Cf. Pischel, Vedische Studien, 1, 175-181.

Vāko-vākya, ‘dialogue,’ is the name given in the Brāhmaṇas to certain portions of the Vedic texts. In one place the brahmodya is said to be a dialogue; very probably in all the passages the brahmodya is meant by this term. Geldner's view is different: he sees in the vākovākya an essential part of the itihāsa-purāṇa, the dialogue or dramatic element as opposed to the narrative portion.
Foot notes Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, iv. 6, 9, 20; xi. 5, 6, 8; 7, 5; Chāndogya upaniṣad, vii. 1, 2, 4; 2, 1; 7, 1.
Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, iv. 6, 9, 20.
Vedische Studien, 1, 291.
Cf. Weber, Indische Studien, 1, 267; Eggeling, Sacred Books of the East, 44, 98, n. 3. It is certain that ‘logic’ is not meant, though Max Müller so renders it in his translation of the Chāndogya upaniṣad.
